1: //! # pathland-host
2: //!
3: //! Host-side reader for the Pathland 16-byte opcode ring. Consumes frames from
4: //! shared linear memory and builds a **native-element description**: the tree
5: //! structure (`TREE`) plus constraint properties (`STYLE`) a renderer maps onto
6: //! that platform's native elements (GTK widgets, DOM elements, HTML).
7: //!
8: //! The engine does not compute layout; this crate stores only what the renderer
9: //! needs to create native elements and let them lay themselves out.
10: 
11: use std::collections::HashMap;
12: 
13: pub use pathland_engine;
14: pub use pathland_opcode;
15: 
16: use pathland_opcode::category;
17: use pathland_opcode::component_type;
18: use pathland_opcode::style;
19: use pathland_opcode::tree;
20: use pathland_opcode::{Frame, Opcode};
21: 
22: /// A decoded node in the host's native-element description.
23: #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
24: pub struct HostNode {
25:     pub id: u32,
26:     pub component_type: u16,
27:     pub text: Option<String>,
28:     pub parent: Option<u32>,
29:     pub children: Vec<u32>,
30:     /// Constraint properties (propertyId → value) for native layout/styling.
31:     pub properties: HashMap<u16, u32>,
32: }
33: 
34: impl Default for HostNode {
35:     fn default() -> Self {
36:         Self {
37:             id: 0,
38:             component_type: component_type::HSTACK,
39:             text: None,
40:             parent: None,
41:             children: Vec::new(),
42:             properties: HashMap::new(),
43:         }
44:     }
45: }
46: 
47: /// The host's native-element description of a rendered tree.
48: #[derive(Debug, Default)]
49: pub struct RenderTree {
50:     /// nodeId → node.
51:     pub nodes: HashMap<u32, HostNode>,
52: }
53: 
54: impl RenderTree {
55:     /// Apply a frame's opcodes to this tree (a delta).
56:     pub fn apply_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) {
57:         for op in frame.opcodes() {
58:             match (op.category(), op.command()) {
59:                 (category::TREE, tree::CREATE_NODE) => {
60:                     let id = op.a();
61:                     let ty = op.b() as u16;
62:                     let entry = self.nodes.entry(id).or_default();
63:                     entry.id = id;
64:                     entry.component_type = ty;
65:                 }
66:                 (category::TREE, tree::DELETE_NODE) => {
67:                     self.nodes.remove(&op.a());
68:                 }
69:                 (category::TREE, tree::INSERT_CHILD) => {
70:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
71:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
72:                         if !p.children.contains(&child) {
73:                             p.children.push(child);
74:                         }
75:                     }
76:                     if let Some(c) = self.nodes.get_mut(&child) {
77:                         c.parent = Some(parent);
78:                     }
79:                 }
80:                 (category::TREE, tree::REMOVE_CHILD) => {
81:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
82:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
83:                         p.children.retain(|c| *c != child);
84:                     }
85:                     if let Some(c) = self.nodes.get_mut(&child) {
86:                         c.parent = None;
87:                     }
88:                 }
89:                 (category::TREE, tree::MOVE_CHILD) => {
90:                     let (parent, child, new_index) = (op.a(), op.b(), op.c() as usize);
91:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
92:                         if let Some(pos) = p.children.iter().position(|c| *c == child) {
93:                             p.children.remove(pos);
94:                         }
95:                         let idx = if new_index == usize::MAX {
96:                             p.children.len()
97:                         } else {
98:                             new_index.min(p.children.len())
99:                         };
100:                         p.children.insert(idx, child);
101:                     }
102:                 }
103:                 (category::STYLE, style::SET_PROPERTY) => {
104:                     let prop_id = op.b() as u16;
105:                     if let Some(n) = self.nodes.get_mut(&op.a()) {
106:                         n.properties.insert(prop_id, op.c());
107:                     }
108:                 }
109:                 (category::STYLE, style::SET_TEXT) => {
110:                     if let Some(n) = self.nodes.get_mut(&op.a()) {
111:                         n.text = frame.arena_str(op.b()).ok().map(|s| s.to_string());
112:                     }
113:                 }
114:                 (category::STYLE, style::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN) => {
115:                     // Token overrides are handled by the renderer's theme layer.
116:                     let _ = op;
117:                 }
118:                 _ => {}
119:             }
120:         }
121:     }
122: 
123:     /// Look up a node by id.
124:     pub fn node(&self, id: u32) -> Option<&HostNode> {
125:         self.nodes.get(&id)
126:     }
127: 
128:     /// The root node (id 0).
129:     pub fn root(&self) -> Option<&HostNode> {
130:         self.nodes.get(&0)
131:     }
132: }
133: 
134: /// Decode a frame into a fresh `RenderTree`.
135: pub fn render_tree_from_frame(frame: &Frame<'_>) -> RenderTree {
136:     let mut tree = RenderTree::default();
137:     tree.apply_frame(frame);
138:     tree
139: }
140: 
141: /// Convert a single opcode into a human-readable line (debugging aid).
142: pub fn describe(op: &Opcode) -> String {
143:     match (op.category(), op.command()) {
144:         (category::TREE, tree::CREATE_NODE) => {
145:             format!("TREE:CREATE_NODE id={} type=0x{:04x}", op.a(), op.b() as u16)
146:         }
147:         (category::TREE, tree::DELETE_NODE) => format!("TREE:DELETE_NODE id={}", op.a()),
148:         (category::TREE, tree::INSERT_CHILD) => format!(
149:             "TREE:INSERT_CHILD parent={} child={} index={}",
150:             op.a(),
151:             op.b(),
152:             op.c()
153:         ),
154:         (category::TREE, tree::REMOVE_CHILD) => {
155:             format!("TREE:REMOVE_CHILD parent={} child={}", op.a(), op.b())
156:         }
157:         (category::TREE, tree::MOVE_CHILD) => format!(
158:             "TREE:MOVE_CHILD parent={} child={} index={}",
159:             op.a(),
160:             op.b(),
161:             op.c()
162:         ),
163:         (category::STYLE, style::SET_PROPERTY) => format!(
164:             "STYLE:SET_PROPERTY id={} prop=0x{:04x} value=0x{:08x}",
165:             op.a(),
166:             op.b() as u16,
167:             op.c()
168:         ),
169:         (category::STYLE, style::SET_TEXT) => {
170:             format!("STYLE:SET_TEXT id={} arenaRef={}", op.a(), op.b())
171:         }
172:         _ => format!("{:?}", op),
173:     }
174: }

1: //! Transport abstraction: how opcode batches move from producer to consumer.
2: //!
3: //! The UI runtime produces renderer-neutral opcodes and knows nothing about the
4: //! transport. This module defines the boundary between:
5: //!
6: //! - the **producer** (opcode engine) that emits opcodes, and
7: //! - the **consumer** (driver) that reads them.
8: //!
9: //! Local transports (shared-memory ring) may be zero-copy; remote transports
10: //! (WebSocket/IPC) copy and serialize. Both conform to the same traits.
11: //!
12: //! The two ends are deliberately separate because a transport is often split
13: //! across a process/IPC boundary, with different backpressure and blocking
14: //! semantics on each side.
15: 
16: use pathland_opcode::Frame;
17: 
18: /// A single in-memory transport unit: one frame of opcodes + arena plus
19: /// transport metadata. Distinct from the raw opcode stream and from the
20: /// wire-format batch.
21: pub struct OpcodeBatch<'a> {
22:     frame: Frame<'a>,
23:     /// Transport direction bitmask (see [`crate::direction`]).
24:     direction: u16,
25: }
26: 
27: impl<'a> OpcodeBatch<'a> {
28:     /// Wrap a frame as a transport batch (guest → host by default).
29:     pub fn new(frame: Frame<'a>, direction: u16) -> Self {
30:         Self { frame, direction }
31:     }
32: 
33:     /// The frame carried by this batch.
34:     pub fn frame(&self) -> &Frame<'a> {
35:         &self.frame
36:     }
37: 
38:     /// Transport direction bitmask.
39:     pub fn direction(&self) -> u16 {
40:         self.direction
41:     }
42: }
43: 
44: /// Errors produced by a transport while sending or receiving.
45: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
46: pub enum TransportError {
47:     /// The consumer has not drained; the producer should retain and retry.
48:     Backpressure,
49:     /// The transport is closed/terminated.
50:     Closed,
51:     /// The peer violated the protocol.
52:     Protocol(ProtocolError),
53: }
54: 
55: /// Sub-errors for protocol violations.
56: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
57: pub enum ProtocolError {
58:     /// The remote sent a version this side does not support.
59:     BadVersion,
60:     /// The payload is malformed (bad magic, truncated, bad length).
61:     Malformed,
62:     /// A raw input could not be interpreted.
63:     BadInput,
64: }
65: 
66: /// Handles raw-input events arriving from the host (renderer → engine).
67: ///
68: /// The driver resolves a raw input to a node id (via hit-testing) and dispatches
69: /// it here; the transport's guest side forwards it to the guest engine.
70: pub trait InputSink {
71:     /// Deliver a raw input (host → guest).
72:     fn dispatch(&mut self, event: &pathland_opcode::Event);
73: }
74: 
75: /// The consumer side of a transport: the driver reads frames here.
76: ///
77: /// A transport may be blocking or non-blocking; `next_frame` reflects that.
78: /// The returned `Frame` borrows the transport's backing memory (zero-copy when
79: /// possible); consume it before the next call.
80: pub trait FrameSource {
81:     /// Read the next available frame, or `None` if none is ready.
82:     ///
83:     /// Blocking vs non-blocking semantics are transport-specific (documented
84:     /// per implementation).
85:     fn next_frame(&mut self) -> Result<Option<OpcodeBatch<'_>>, TransportError>;
86: }
87: 
88: /// A consumer-side transport that can also send raw inputs back to the guest.
89: pub trait DriverTransport: FrameSource {
90:     /// Send a raw input from the host to the guest over this transport.
91:     fn send_input(&mut self, event: &pathland_opcode::Event) -> Result<(), TransportError>;
92: }

1: //! Shared-memory ring transport (zero-copy, SPSC).
2: //!
3: //! The producer (opcode engine) and consumer (native driver) share one linear
4: //! memory buffer containing the ring + arena. The producer writes 16-byte
5: //! opcodes via `pathland_opcode::Guest`; the consumer reads completed frames via
6: //! `pathland_opcode::Host`. No copying, no batching, no serialization — this is
7: //! the high-performance local path.
8: 
9: use pathland_opcode::{init_memory, Guest, Host, MemoryLayout};
10: 
11: use crate::traits::{DriverTransport, FrameSource, OpcodeBatch, TransportError};
12: 
13: /// A zero-copy SPSC shared-memory ring transport.
14: ///
15: /// Owns the linear-memory buffer (header + ring + arena). Producers and
16: /// consumers are granted short-lived `Guest`/`Host` views over the same buffer
17: /// via the borrowed methods, so opcodes flow in place with no copies.
18: #[derive(Debug)]
19: pub struct RingTransport {
20:     /// Shared linear memory (header | ring | arena).
21:     mem: Vec<u8>,
22:     /// Ring/arena geometry.
23:     layout: MemoryLayout,
24: }
25: 
26: impl RingTransport {
27:     /// Create a ring transport with a default layout and a zeroed header.
28:     pub fn new() -> Self {
29:         let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
30:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
31:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
32:         Self { mem, layout }
33:     }
34: 
35:     /// Create a ring transport over a caller-provided buffer/layout.

## What's wrong

1. **No standalone GTK renderer exists.** The GTK widget-mapping logic is inlined in `pathland-gtk-demo/src/main.rs` (`render_node`, `spacing`, `apply_text_style`). It's demo code, not a reusable renderer — so it can't be shared.

3. **The demos reach past Pathland.** The Rust demo authors its tree with Pathland, but then hand-builds GTK widgets; the Java demo builds its tree with Pathland but renders with Swing. Neither renders through a Pathland renderer.

## What's already there (good foundation)

- `pathland-host::RenderTree` — renderer-neutral decode of opcode frames into a tree (`id → component_type/text/properties/children`). This is exactly what a renderer consumes.
- `pathland-native` — a `cdylib` C-ABI shim + `NativeHost` (retained tree + engine + zero-copy ring) that Java already drives via JNA.
- `pathland-opcode::Event` + `InputSink` — the raw-input event model (renderer → app), currently stubbed for the ring transport.

## Proposed target architecture

A single shared **`pathland-gtk`** crate (new) that owns *all* GTK usage:

```
pathland-gtk (rlib + cdylib)
  GtkRenderer { tree: RenderTree, widgets: HashMap<u32, gtk::Widget> }
    - apply_frame(&Frame)   // opcode delta → GTK widget delta
    - root_widget() -> gtk::Widget

## Recommendation

**In-process via JNA.** With events in place, event ingress is just a JNA `Callback` (GTK button → `void onActivated(int nodeId)` → Java), so there's no reason to build a separate renderer process or a bidirectional IPC transport. Both demos then share the *identical* Rust `pathland-gtk` renderer — the Rust demo links it as an `rlib`, Java loads it as a `cdylib` through the existing `pathland-native`/JNA pattern.

---

# Plan: Shared GTK renderer + two GTK demos (no Swing)

## Target architecture

```
pathland-view (DSL) ── pathland-engine ── ring ──▶ pathland-gtk (GTK renderer)
                                                        ▲
pathland-native (C ABI, NativeHost + ring) ─────────────┘
    Rust demo: DSL → engine → ring → GtkRenderer::run(...)      (no gtk imports)
    Java demo: DSL → pathland-native → pathland_gtk_run(...)    (no Swing/gtk imports)
```

`pathland-gtk` is the single owner of all `gtk::`/`glib::`/`pango::` usage.

## 1. New crate `lib/rust/crates/pathland-gtk/` (rlib + cdylib)

- **Deps**: `pathland-opcode`, `pathland-host` (RenderTree), `pathland-transport` (FrameSource), `pathland-native` (only for the C-ABI glue), `gtk4`, `glib`, `pango`.
- **`GtkRenderer`** (transport-agnostic core):
  - `GtkRenderer::new(on_activated)` where `on_activated: Box<dyn FnMut(u32)>` (node id on button activation).
  - `apply_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame)` — `RenderTree::apply_frame` + sync the `id → gtk::Widget` map (create/delete/update native widgets; rebuild-from-tree is acceptable for the first cut, incremental later).
  - `run(app_id, title, source: &mut dyn FrameSource, on_activated)` — owns `gtk::Application`/`ApplicationWindow`, installs a `glib` idle callback that drains `source` and calls `apply_frame` (the frame pump), connects `BUTTON` widgets' `clicked` → `on_activated(node_id)`, and runs the main loop. The demo never touches GTK.
- **C ABI** (Java glue): `pathland_gtk_run(host: HostHandle, on_activated: Option<extern "C" fn(u32)>)` — casts the opaque `NativeHost` handle, wraps it as a `FrameSource`, and delegates to `GtkRenderer::run`. A second function `pathland_gtk_free`/destroy if needed for lifetime.

## 2. `pathland-native` — expose the host as a `FrameSource`

- Add `impl FrameSource for NativeHost` (`next_frame()` forwards to the internal `RingTransport`), so the renderer can drain frames from the same host Java keeps calling `emit()` on. This is the missing piece that lets an interactive Java app keep re-emitting while the renderer reads deltas.

## 3. Event ingress (native path)

- GTK `BUTTON` mapping connects `connect_clicked` → `on_activated(node_id)`.
- Rust demo: closure mutates `count`, rebuilds DSL, `engine.emit` into the ring; the renderer's idle pump picks up the next frame.
- Java demo: JNA `Callback` (kept alive via a strong ref) does the same via `bridge.importTreeAndEmit`; the in-process renderer reads the host's ring.
- Note: this is a pragmatic "activated(id)" signal for the demo. Full raw-input `EVENT` opcodes (pointer-down/up with coords) stay deferred — worth calling out in AGENTS.md.

## 4. Rust demo `pathland-gtk-demo` — remove direct GTK

- Delete all `gtk`/`glib`/`pango` imports and `render_node`/`spacing`/`apply_text_style`.
- `main()` becomes: hold `Engine` + `RingTransport` + `count`, author the DSL, then `GtkRenderer::run(APP_ID, "Pathland GTK4 Demo", &mut ring, |id| { count += 1; re-emit(); })`.
- `Cargo.toml`: drop `gtk/glib/pango`; depend on `pathland-gtk`.

## 5. Java demo — remove Swing, use the GTK renderer

- **Delete** `demo/DemoApp.java` (Swing).
- **Add** `pathland/PathlandGtk.java` — JNA interface mapping `pathland_gtk_run` (and the event callback type).
- **Add** `demo/GtkDemo.java` — authors the Pathland DSL (same counter UI), `bridge.importTreeAndEmit`, then `PathlandGtk.INSTANCE.pathland_gtk_run(host, this::onActivated)`; `onActivated(id)` increments and re-emits. No `javax.swing`/`java.awt` anywhere.
- `DemoHeadless.java` stays (headless DSL→ring verification, no rendering).
- `pom.xml`: default `exec.mainClass` → `demo.GtkDemo`.
- `pathland-native` + `pathland-gtk` must both be built before `mvn`; `jna.library.path` already points at `target/debug`.

- `lib/rust/README.md`: add `pathland-gtk` to the crate list and the GTK demo run instructions.

- `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (all crates; `pathland-gtk` tests: `apply_frame` builds the right widget tree).
- `cargo build -p pathland-native -p pathland-gtk`.
- Rust demo: `cargo run -p pathland-gtk-demo` (counter renders + increments).
- Java demo: `mvn ... compile exec:java` (default `GtkDemo`) renders + increments; `-Dexec.mainClass=demo.DemoHeadless` still prints `OK: ... 'Count: 8'`.

19: /// `slots` is the full ring region; `mask` wraps the cursor. Fails with
20: /// `RingError::Full` when the next slot equals `readCursor`.
21: #[inline]
22: pub(crate) fn push(slots: &mut [u8], header: &mut [u8], mask: usize, op: &Opcode) -> Result<(), RingError> {
23:     let write = cursor(header, memory::OFF_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
24:     let next = (write + 1) & mask;
25:     if next == cursor(header, memory::OFF_READ_CURSOR, mask) {
26:         return Err(RingError::Full);
27:     }
28:     let bytes = op.to_bytes();
29:     let off = write * Opcode::SIZE;
30:     slots[off..off + Opcode::SIZE].copy_from_slice(&bytes);
31:     header::set_u32(header, memory::OFF_WRITE_CURSOR, next as u32);
32:     Ok(())
33: }

35: /// Read the current cursor value for a header offset, masked.
36: #[inline]
37: pub(crate) fn cursor(header: &[u8], off: usize, mask: usize) -> usize {
38:     header::get_u32(header, off) as usize & mask
39: }

93:     pub fn new(mem: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
94:         Self { mem }

97:     fn u32(&self, off: usize) -> u32 {

285: /// A completed frame produced by the guest: a sequence of opcodes plus arena
286: /// access.
287: ///
288: /// `Frame` is the **transport seam**: both the shared-memory ring (`Host`) and
289: /// network batch decoders produce frame views, so consumers such as
290: /// `RenderTree::apply_frame` work identically regardless of origin.
291: pub struct Frame<'a> {
292:     slots: &'a [u8],
293:     arena: &'a [u8],
294:     start: usize,
295:     end: usize,
296: }
297: 
298: impl<'a> Frame<'a> {
299:     /// Construct a frame view over contiguous 16-byte opcode slots plus an
300:     /// arena region (`start`/`end` are byte offsets into `slots`).
301:     ///
302:     /// Used by transport backends to produce `Frame` views over their own
303:     /// buffers; `Host` builds these internally from the ring.
304:     pub fn from_parts(slots: &'a [u8], arena: &'a [u8], start: usize, end: usize) -> Self {
305:         Self {
306:             slots,
307:             arena,
308:             start,
309:             end,
310:         }
311:     }
312: 
313:     /// Iterate the opcodes in this frame, in order.
314:     pub fn opcodes(&self) -> FrameIter<'a> {
315:         FrameIter {
316:             slots: self.slots,
317:             cursor: self.start,
318:             end: self.end,
319:         }
320:     }
321: 
322:     /// Number of opcodes in the frame.
323:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
324:         (self.end - self.start) / Opcode::SIZE
325:     }
326: 
327:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
328:         self.len() == 0
329:     }
330: 
331:     /// Read an arena entry by offset (see `Guest::alloc` / `Guest::alloc_str`).
332:     pub fn arena_get(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a [u8], ArenaError> {
333:         arena_fn::get(self.arena, offset)
334:     }
335: 
336:     /// Read an arena string by offset.
337:     pub fn arena_str(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a str, ArenaError> {
338:         arena_fn::get_str(self.arena, offset)
339:     }
340: 
341:     /// The full arena region (for transport serialization of arena deltas).
342:     pub fn arena(&self) -> &'a [u8] {
343:         self.arena
344:     }
345: }
346: 
347: /// Iterator over the opcodes in a `Frame`.
348: pub struct FrameIter<'a> {
349:     slots: &'a [u8],
350:     cursor: usize,
351:     end: usize,
352: }
353: 
354: impl<'a> Iterator for FrameIter<'a> {
355:     type Item = Opcode;
356: 
357:     fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Opcode> {
358:         if self.cursor >= self.end {
359:             return None;
360:         }
361:         let bytes: [u8; 16] = self.slots[self.cursor..self.cursor + 16].try_into().unwrap();
362:         self.cursor += 16;
363:         Some(Opcode::from_bytes(&bytes))
364:     }
365: }

367: /// Consumer side: the host renderer reading completed frames.
368: ///
369: /// SPSC contract: the host never reads past the producer's published
370: /// `writeCursor`, and the producer never overwrites an unconsumed `readCursor`.
371: /// If the host is slow, multiple produced frames are coalesced into one `Frame`
372: /// (opcodes remain in order); the `frameCount` simply signals "new data".
373: pub struct Host<'a> {
374:     header: &'a mut [u8],
375:     slots: &'a [u8],
376:     arena: &'a [u8],
377:     /// Number of frames already consumed by this host view.
378:     consumed: u32,
379: }
380: 
381: impl<'a> Host<'a> {
382:     /// Create a host view over the linear memory.
383:     pub fn new(mem: &'a mut [u8], layout: &MemoryLayout) -> Self {
384:         let (header, rest) = mem.split_at_mut(memory::HEADER_SIZE);
385:         let (slots, arena) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.ring_bytes());
386:         Self {
387:             header,
388:             slots,
389:             arena,
390:             consumed: 0,
391:         }
392:     }
393: 
394:     /// Total frames produced by the guest (for diagnostics).
395:     pub fn frame_count(&self) -> u32 {
396:         header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT)
397:     }
398: 
399:     /// Consume all frames produced since the last call, advancing `readCursor`.
400:     ///
401:     /// Returns at most one `Frame` (all new opcodes since the last drain). If
402:     /// the producer produced multiple frames before this call they coalesce.
403:     pub fn frames(&mut self) -> Vec<Frame<'a>> {
404:         let frame_count = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT);
405:         if self.consumed >= frame_count {
406:             return Vec::new();
407:         }
408:         let mask = slot_mask(self.header);
409:         let start = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, mask);
410:         let end = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
411: 
412:         // The POC producer flushes before the ring fills, so `end >= start`
413:         // always holds. Guard against a wrapped ring by draining nothing; a
414:         // wrapped producer must flush first (see OPCODE.md backpressure).
415:         if end < start {
416:             return Vec::new();
417:         }
418: 
419:         let frames = vec![Frame {
420:             slots: self.slots,
421:             arena: self.arena,
422:             start: start * Opcode::SIZE,
423:             end: end * Opcode::SIZE,
424:         }];
425: 
426:         header::set_u32(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, end as u32);
427:         self.consumed = frame_count;
428:         frames
429:     }
430: }

200: engine's next `emit` reconciles and writes only the delta. The renderer applies
201: each frame as a delta to its native elements.
202: 
203: ---
204: 
205: ## Linear Memory Layout
206: 
207: The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:
208: 
209: ```
210: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
211: | 0x0000  Header block (64 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
212: | 0x0040  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)                         |
213: | ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
214: | 0x10040 Arena (bump region for strings / token paths / lists)  |
215: | ...                                                            |
216: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
217: ```
218: 
219: ### Header block (64 bytes)
220: 
221: | Offset | Size | Field | Producer | Description |
222: |--------|------|-------|----------|-------------|
223: | 0x00 | 4 | `magic` | — | `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`) |
224: | 0x04 | 2 | `version` | — | Wire protocol version (1) |
225: | 0x06 | 4 | `ringOffset` | — | Byte offset of the ring region |
226: | 0x0A | 4 | `ringBytes` | — | Byte length of the ring region |
227: | 0x0E | 4 | `slotCount` | — | Number of ring slots (power of two) |
228: | 0x12 | 4 | `arenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the arena region |
229: | 0x16 | 4 | `arenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the arena region |
230: | 0x1A | 4 | `arenaCursor` | guest | Next free byte in the arena |
231: | 0x1E | 4 | `readCursor` | host | Ring slot the host has consumed up to |
232: | 0x22 | 4 | `writeCursor` | guest | Ring slot the guest has written up to |
233: | 0x26 | 4 | `frameCount` | guest | Monotonic completed-frame counter |
234: | 0x2A | 22 | reserved | — | Zero |
235: 
236: ### Ring buffer
237: 
238: - Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
239: - **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
240: - **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
241: - **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
242: - **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.
243: 
244: ### Arena
245: 
246: - A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
247: - Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
248: - Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
249: - The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.
250: 
251: ---
252: 
253: ## Colors
254: 
255: Literal colors are **sRGB** (IEC 61966-2-1, D65 white point), packed as `0xAARRGGBB`:
256: 
257: - `AA`: alpha (0x00 transparent – 0xFF opaque)
258: - `RR`: red, `GG`: green, `BB`: blue
259: 
260: Stored little-endian in a `u32` payload. Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation remain **renderer-owned** (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).
261: 
262: ---
263: 
264: ## Design Token System
265: 
266: ### Core Principle
267: 
268: > **The renderer owns the defaults. The application owns the overrides.**
269: 
270: This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency when the application overrides tokens.
271: 
272: ### Responsibilities
273: 
274: | Aspect | Owner | Responsibility |
275: |--------|-------|----------------|
276: | **Default Token Values** | Renderer | Define platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens |
277: | **Token Overrides** | Application | Specify overrides for cross-platform consistency |
278: | **Token Resolution** | Renderer | Resolve final token values (override or default) |
279: | **Platform Adaptation** | Renderer | Adapt default token values to platform conventions |
280: 
281: ### Token Identification
282: 
283: Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`, `font.body`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.
284: 
285: ### Token Resolution Algorithm
286: 
287: ```
288: FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath: string) -> PropertyValue:
289:     IF applicationOverrides.has(tokenPath):
290:         RETURN applicationOverrides[tokenPath]
291:     ELSE IF rendererDefaults.has(tokenPath):
292:         RETURN rendererDefaults[tokenPath]
293:     ELSE IF hasParentToken(tokenPath):
294:         RETURN resolveToken(getParentPath(tokenPath))
295:     ELSE:
296:         RETURN getFallbackValue(tokenPath)
297: ```
298: 
299: ### Renderer Responsibilities
300: 
301: The renderer MUST:
302: 
303: 1. Provide platform-appropriate defaults for all standard tokens (e.g. `color.primary`, `font.body.size`, `space.md`).
304: 2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
305: 3. Resolve design-token references in properties.
306: 4. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
307: 5. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.
308: 
309: The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume specific default token values.
310: 
311: ### Standard Token Catalog
312: 
313: Required core tokens (renderer MUST support with platform-appropriate defaults): `color.primary`, `color.secondary`, `color.background`, `color.surface`, `color.text.primary`, `color.text.secondary`, `color.border`, `font.body.size`, `font.body.weight`, `font.body.family`, `space.xs`–`space.lg`.
314: 
315: Recommended extended tokens: `color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`, `font.heading.1`–`font.heading.6`, `font.size.heading.1`–`6`, `radius.sm`/`md`, `elevation.low`/`high`, `opacity.disabled`.
316: 
317: ---
318: 
319: ## Frame Lifecycle
320: 
321: A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:
322: 
323: 1. Guest begins a frame.
324: 2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
325: 3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
326: 4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
327: 5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.
328: 
329: Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.

## Answer on events

You're right — as planned, the GTK renderer would have handed button clicks straight back through a Rust closure / JNA callback. That's a side-channel, and it violates the "both directions are binary, renderers are dumb" principle. Events should travel as **16-byte `EVENT` opcodes through the opcode engine**, exactly like `TREE`/`STYLE` do.

The reason they don't today: the shared memory has **only a guest→host ring** (`Guest` writes, `Host` reads). The `EVENT` opcode format already exists (`Event::encode` → `Opcode`, `Event::try_from`), but there's no **host→guest channel** to carry it — `RingTransport::send_input` is literally stubbed to `BadInput`. So the missing piece is a **second ring for the host→guest direction**.

# Plan (revised): shared GTK renderer + bidirectional opcode events

## A. Host→guest event ring in `pathland-opcode`

Make events flow through the engine as opcodes:

- **Memory layout**: header (64 B) | ring (guest→host, `slotCount`×16) | **event ring** (host→guest, `slotCount`×16) | arena. Reuse `slotCount` for both rings (no new `MemoryLayout` field; only `total_bytes`/`arena_offset` shift).
- **Header** (uses the 22 reserved bytes at `0x2A`):
  - `0x2A eventRingOffset`, `0x2E eventRingBytes`, `0x32 eventSlotCount`, `0x36 eventReadCursor` (guest-owned), `0x3A eventWriteCursor` (host-owned), `0x3E` reserved.
- **New writer/reader**: a `HostWriter` (renderer writes `Event::encode()` opcodes) and a `GuestReader` (guest drains + `Event::try_from`). Add `push_event`/`drain_events` to the ring module.
- **Spec**: update `spec/OPCODE.md` memory-layout section + conformance vector for the event-ring header init. `EVENT` opcode byte format itself is unchanged.

## B. Transport: make the ring bidirectional

- `RingTransport::send_input(&Event)` — actually writes the encoded EVENT opcode into the event ring (currently `BadInput`).
- Add `RingTransport::drain_events() -> Vec<Event>` (guest side reads + decodes).
- The renderer's idle pump runs both: read guest→host frames, and after rendering, drain events and dispatch to the app.

## C. `pathland-native` — expose both directions to Java

- `impl FrameSource for NativeHost` (`next_frame`), `send_input(&Event)`, `drain_events()`.
- C ABI: `pathland_gtk_run(host, on_event_cb)` where `on_event_cb` is a JNA callback `void onEvent(int targetId)` (kept alive by Java). The renderer, in-process, pumps the host's ring: renders frames and dispatches decoded `EVENT` opcodes back to Java.

## D. New `pathland-gtk` crate (rlib + cdylib) — **incremental**

- `GtkRenderer { tree: RenderTree, widgets: HashMap<u32, gtk::Widget>, on_event }`.
- `apply_frame(&Frame)` applies the **delta** to `RenderTree` and mutates the `id → gtk::Widget` map incrementally: `CREATE_NODE`/`INSERT_CHILD` build the widget and attach it; `DELETE_NODE`/`REMOVE_CHILD` drop it; `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT` update the existing widget in place (`gtk::Widget::set_*`, Pango attrs). No full rebuild.
- `run(app_id, title, source, on_event)` owns `gtk::Application`/`ApplicationWindow`, installs a `glib` idle pump: drain `source` → `apply_frame`, drain events → `on_event(Event)`. `BUTTON` widgets connect `clicked` → `send_input(Event::PointerUp{ target, .. })`.
- C ABI `pathland_gtk_run(host, on_event_cb)` reuses the `NativeHost` as the bidirectional source.

## E. Demos — no GTK/Swing in demo code

- **Rust** `pathland-gtk-demo`: drop all `gtk`/`glib`/`pango` imports and the inline `render_node`; hold `Engine` + `RingTransport` + `count`, author the DSL, then `GtkRenderer::run(APP_ID, title, &mut ring, |event| { count += 1; re-emit(); })`.
- **Java**: delete `demo/DemoApp.java` (Swing); add `pathland/PathlandGtk.java` (JNA: `pathland_gtk_run` + event callback) and `demo/GtkDemo.java` (Pathland DSL → `bridge.importTreeAndEmit` → `PathlandGtk.run(host, this::onEvent)`; `onEvent(id)` increments + re-emits). No `javax.swing`/`java.awt` anywhere. `DemoHeadless` stays; `pom.xml` default `exec.mainClass` → `demo.GtkDemo`.

## F. Docs & verify

- `AGENTS.md`: document `pathland-gtk`, the no-Swing / demos-never-touch-GTK rule, and the bidirectional event ring.
- Verify: `cargo test` (opcode ring round-trip incl. event direction, renderer delta tests), `cargo build -p pathland-native -p pathland-gtk`, `cargo run -p pathland-gtk-demo` (counter increments), `mvn ... exec:java` (`GtkDemo`) + `-Dexec.mainClass=demo.DemoHeadless` (still `OK: ... 'Count: 8'`).

---

One scoping note before I start: the event ring is a **wire/memory-format change** (new header fields + a second ring region). It's pre-release so it stays version 1, but it touches `pathland-opcode`'s layout, conformance vectors, and the WASM guest's memory init (which uses the same layout). I'll update all of those consistently. Want me to proceed with this full scope, or limit the first pass to the in-process Rust demo event loop and layer the Java event path in a follow-up?
Will the opcodes stay 16-byte fixed for each meeeage?

Yes. Every opcode — `TREE`, `STYLE`, `EVENT`, `META` — stays exactly **16 bytes**:

```
Category (1B) | Command (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)
```

Events are no exception: `Event::encode()` produces a plain 16-byte `Opcode` (same struct the TREE/STYLE path uses), and `Event::try_from` decodes it. The event ring I proposed is just a **second array of 16-byte slots** in shared memory — identical slot layout to the main ring, just a different producer/consumer direction.

This is a non-negotiable invariant, and my plan preserves it:

- The event-ring **header fields** are fixed-size `u32`s (4 bytes each), not opcodes.
- Variable-length data (strings, token paths) still goes in the **arena** and is referenced by `u32` offset inside the opcode — never inline.
- Nothing in the event ring, incremental renderer, or the Java path changes opcode size or introduces variable-length messages.

The only thing that changes is *where* a second 16-byte-slot region lives in linear memory (and the header cursors to track it).
And that header is for the buffer ring transport? Not other transports?

Correct — the 64-byte header block is specific to the **shared-memory ring transport**. It's the in-memory layout (`header | ring | arena`) that the zero-copy ring (`RingTransport` / foreign drivers like the Java `RingReader`) uses.

What's universal vs. transport-specific:

| Thing | Scope |
|---|---|
| 16-byte opcodes (`TREE`/`STYLE`/`EVENT`/`META`) | **Transport-agnostic** — identical bytes in the ring and in a network batch |
| Header block (cursors, `frameCount`, ring/arena geometry) | **Ring transport only** |
| Network batch envelope (`magic PLPL`, version, flags, frameCount, opcodeCount, opcodes, arenaDelta) | **Network transport only** (`NetBatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder`) |

So the event ring + its `eventReadCursor`/`eventWriteCursor` header fields I proposed live in the **shared-memory ring layout only**. The 16-byte `EVENT` opcodes themselves are universal; a future remote host would carry those same opcodes over the network batch wire format (or a separate host→guest batch channel), not via the ring header.

The transport seam is `Frame`/`OpcodeBatch` (`FrameSource`/`DriverTransport`) — a driver consumes frames/events regardless of origin, which is exactly why the GTK renderer can stay transport-agnostic and only the C-ABI glue (`pathland_gtk_run`) knows it's a ring.
There reason that the opcode is 16byte is to ensure performance across processors and platforms fx. RiscV rva 23, esp32, Apple M processors, intel, amd etc. Is this still ensured?

Yes — fully ensured, and my plan doesn't change any of it. Here's why the 16-byte guarantee is architecture-independent, confirmed against the actual code:

**1. Fixed-width types, language-guaranteed sizes.** The opcode is `u8 | u8 | u16 | u32 | u32 | u32`. In Rust, `u8`/`u16`/`u32` are *always* 1/2/4 bytes on every target — RISC-V (rv64 / RV A23), ESP32 (Xtensa and RISC-V), ARM64 (Apple M), x86, AMD. `f32` is always IEEE-754 binary32. Nothing here is `usize`, pointer-sized, or C `int`-sized, which is what would vary per platform.

**2. `#[repr(C, packed)]` guarantees exactly 16 bytes, no padding.** There's a test `size_is_16_bytes` asserting `size_of::<Opcode>() == 16`. Packed repr eliminates any compiler-inserted alignment padding, so the size is identical across every ABI.

**3. Alignment-independence.** Because it's packed, fields may be unaligned — the accessors use `ptr::addr_of!(...).read_unaligned()` (opcode.rs:73–94), which is well-defined on all targets, including ones that fault on misaligned loads (older ARM, some RISC-V configs). No reliance on natural alignment.

**5. No pointers, no padding-sensitive payloads.** Opcodes carry only integer/float payloads; variable data (strings/tokens) lives in the arena referenced by a `u32` offset — so the opcode never embeds platform-sized pointers.

2: //!
3: //! Every entry is self-describing: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`. Opcodes
4: //! reference entries by their byte offset (`arenaRef`), so the entry length is

9: /// Errors produced by the arena.
10: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
11: pub enum ArenaError {
12:     /// Not enough remaining bytes for the allocation.
13:     OutOfSpace,
14:     /// The arena offset is out of bounds or points to an invalid entry.
15:     InvalidOffset,
16: }
17: 
18: /// Allocate `bytes` into the arena region, returning its byte offset.
19: ///
20: /// The cursor lives in the header block (`OFF_ARENA_CURSOR`).
21: #[inline]
22: pub(crate) fn alloc(data: &mut [u8], header: &mut [u8], bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<u32, ArenaError> {
23:     let cursor = header::get_u32(header, crate::memory::OFF_ARENA_CURSOR) as usize;
24:     let len = bytes.len();
25:     let needed = 4 + len;
26:     if cursor + needed > data.len() {
27:         return Err(ArenaError::OutOfSpace);
28:     }
29:     data[cursor..cursor + 4].copy_from_slice(&(len as u32).to_le_bytes());
30:     data[cursor + 4..cursor + needed].copy_from_slice(bytes);
31:     header::set_u32(header, crate::memory::OFF_ARENA_CURSOR, (cursor + needed) as u32);
32:     Ok(cursor as u32)
33: }
34: 
35: /// Allocate a string, returning its arena offset.

37: pub(crate) fn alloc_str(
38:     data: &mut [u8],
39:     header: &mut [u8],
40:     s: &str,
41: ) -> Result<u32, ArenaError> {

43: }

45: /// Read the bytes of the entry at `offset` from an arena region.
46: #[inline]

51:     }
52:     let len = u32::from_le_bytes(data[off..off + 4].try_into().unwrap()) as usize;
53:     if off + 4 + len > data.len() {
54:         return Err(ArenaError::InvalidOffset);
55:     }

57: }

content.text: Now let me add a note about the event ring to the Ring buffer section and Frame Lifecycle. Let me update the "Ring buffer" section to mention the event ring direction:

input.newString:
### Ring buffer

- Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
- **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
- **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
- **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
- **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.

### Event ring (host → guest)

- The **host** (renderer) is the producer: it writes `EVENT`-category opcodes at `eventWriteCursor`.
- The **guest** (app/engine) is the consumer: it reads from `eventReadCursor` up to `eventWriteCursor`, then advances `eventReadCursor`.
- Events are raw inputs and are consumed as soon as they are written (no frame batching); `eventFrameCount` is not required.
- Backpressure mirrors the main ring: the host must not advance `eventWriteCursor` past `eventReadCursor`.

1: # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
2: 
3: This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
4: 
5: **Last Updated**: August 14, 2026
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## New Direction: Rust WASM Opcode Engine
10: 
11: > The canonical core is a **Rust engine compiled to WASM** ("WASM guest engine")
12: > that emits the application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack,
13: > Text, spacing, padding, alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer**
14: > into shared linear memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and
15: > modifiers are written in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API; other languages consume
16: > the components as **WASM/WIT** components.
17: 
18: ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
19: 
20: - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
21: - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
22: - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
23: - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes.
24: - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors).
25: 
26: ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
27: 
28: > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
29: > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
30: > not emit rects.**
31: 
32: - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`STYLE` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
33: - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
34: - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
35: - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
36: 
37: ### Rust Workspace (`lib/rust/`)
38: 
39: ```
40: crates/pathland-opcode/   # 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, memory layout (no_std)
41: crates/pathland-view/     # SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text/Button +
42:                           #   decoupled modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/
43:                           #   background) + vstack!/hstack! macros (no_std)
44: crates/pathland-engine/   # retained view tree -> declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes,
45:                           #   diff-based reactive emission (zero-alloc steady state)
46: crates/pathland-host/     # host reader: ring -> native-element description (std layer)
47: crates/pathland-transport/# opcode transport: shared-memory ring + network batch
48:                           #   encode/decode + batching policy + transport abstraction (std)
49: crates/pathland-guest/    # WASM guest component (wit world): retained tree + engine
50:                           #   + emit/take-batch + event ingress (wasm32-wasip1, browser)
51: crates/pathland-wit-host/ # WIT host bindings + DSL bridge (wasmtime embed, remote hosts)
52: crates/pathland-native/   # NATIVE C-ABI shim + NativeHost: flat world over a zero-copy
53:                           #   shared-memory ring, for Swift/Java/C#/other native hosts
54: crates/pathland-gtk-demo/ # GTK4 desktop demo: native engine -> zero-copy shared ring
55:                           #   -> GtkBox/Label/Button (no WASM on desktop)
56: wit/pathland.wit          # WIT component-world definitions
57: lib/java/pathland-demo/   # Java (Maven) demo: SwiftUI-like DSL + JNA over pathland-native,
58:                           #   reading opcodes zero-copy from the shared ring
59: ```
60: 
61: - Test: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all native crates; `pathland-guest` is
62:   wasm-only and ignored by the native build).
63: - WASM component build (browser goal): `cd lib/rust/crates/pathland-guest && cargo component build`
64:   (also needs `PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"` so rustup's `cargo`/`rustc` are used).
65: - Run the GTK demo (native, zero-copy shared ring): `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-gtk-demo`.
66: - Run the Java demo (JNA over the native C-ABI shim):
67:   `PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo build -p pathland-native`
68:   then `cd lib/java/pathland-demo && mvn -q -Dpathland.rust.target=<lib/rust/target/debug> compile exec:java`.
69: 
70: ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-native`)
71: 
72: The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: a native `cdylib` exposing the
73: flat world (same semantics as `wit/pathland.wit`) as `pathland_native_*` C
74: functions, with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
75: language that links the dylib (Swift/Java/C# via FFI) calls the flat surface —
76: no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy. The Java demo
77: (`lib/java/pathland-demo`) demonstrates this with a SwiftUI-like Java DSL over
78: JNA. wasmtime/WIT remain only for remote/browser hosts.
79: 
80: ### WIT Component World (`wit/pathland.wit`)
81: 
82: The `pathland:view/pathland` world is the **language-agnostic surface** other
83: languages (Java/Quarkus, Rust GTK, future hosts) drive. It is flat and id-based,
84: deliberately NOT the Rust DSL:
85: 
86: - `builder`: `create-node(id, component)`, `insert-child`, `remove-child`,
87:   `set-text`, `set-property`. Hosts supply stable node ids — stable ids across
88:   updates are what make the guest's diff-based reactive emission work.
89: - `engine`: `begin-frame`, `emit`, `end-frame`, `take-batch` (returns the
90:   network-batch bytes, so the same wire format serves desktop + network hosts).
91: - `input`: `dispatch(event)` — raw-input event ingress (host → guest).
92: - `app` (imported): `on-event(event)` — the host application callback.
93: 
94: The **DSL is a uniform surface**: a developer authors with `vstack![...]` /
95: `text(...)` / custom views; the bridge (`pathland-wit-host::import_tree`) walks
96: the `Node` tree into `builder` calls. Core (WIT) and custom views are
97: indistinguishable to the developer.
98: 
99: ### POC Goals (issues #12–#18)
100: 
101: | # | Goal | Status |
102: |---|------|--------|
103: | 12 | 16-byte opcode engine | **Complete** |
104: | 13 | Core components & modifiers in Rust | **Complete** |
105: | 18 | Opcode transport layer (+ native C-ABI shim, zero-copy ring) | **Complete** |
106: | 16 | Rust desktop app with GTK4 renderer (native shared ring) | **In progress** |
107: | 15 | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo | Planned |
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ## Project Vision
112: 
113: **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
114: 
115: **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
116: 
117: **Status**: The Rust WASM opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the New Direction section above.
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
122: 
123: ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
124: 
125: > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
126: 
127: - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
128: - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
129: - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
130: - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
131: - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
132: 
133: **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
134: 
135: ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
136: 
137: > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
138: 
139: - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
140: - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
141: - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
142: - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
143: 
144: ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
145: 
146: > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
147: 
148: - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
149: - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
150: - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
151: - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic
152: 
153: ---
154: 
155: ## Protocol Quick Reference
156: 
157: ### Opcode Format
158: 
159: Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
160: 
161: ```
162: [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
163: ```
164: 
165: See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
166: 
167: ### Categories
168: 
169: | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
170: |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
171: | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
172: | STYLE | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
173: | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
174: | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment |
175: 
176: ### Component Types (u16)
177: 
178: | Component | ID |
179: |-----------|----|
180: | HSTACK | 0x0001 |
181: | VSTACK | 0x0002 |
182: | TEXT | 0x0003 |
183: | BUTTON | 0x0004 |
184: | IMAGE | 0x0005 |
185: | SWITCH | 0x0006 |
186: | TEXT_FIELD | 0x0007 |
187: | SPACER | 0x0008 |
188: | SCROLLVIEW | 0x0009 |
189: | LIST | 0x000A |
190: | GRID | 0x000B |
191: | COMMENT | 0x000C |
192: 
193: ### Key Property IDs
194: 
195: **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, JUSTIFICATION=0x0003, PADDING=0x0004, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
196: **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
197: **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
198: **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
199: **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004
200: 
201: ### Colors
202: 
203: - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
204: - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
205: 
206: ### Design Token System
207: 
208: **Core Principle**: Application defines intent and overrides. Renderer defines visual appearance and behavior.
209: 
210: - Renderer owns design tokens, default values, semantic-token resolution, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme logic
211: - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system
212: - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
213: 
214: Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system).
215: 
216: ---
217: 
218: ## Implementation Guidelines
219: 
220: ### Adding New Component
221: 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-opcode/src/constants.rs`
222: 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
223: 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-engine` (if it affects the retained tree)
224: 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
225: 
226: ### Adding New Property
227: 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
228: 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
229: 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-engine`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
230: 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
231: 
232: ### Modifying Protocol
233: 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
234: 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-opcode` encoding/emitters
235: 3. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-engine`/`pathland-host` + tests
236: 
237: ### Changing the Wire Format
238: - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-opcode`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
239: 
240: ---
241: 
242: ## Common Pitfalls
243: 
244: ### NEVER Do These
245: | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
246: |--------------|-----------|---------|
247: | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
248: | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
249: | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
250: | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
251: | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
252: | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
253: | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
254: | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |
255: 
256: ---
257: 
258: ## Project Status
259: 
260: **Complete**: 16-byte opcode engine (`pathland-opcode`), SwiftUI-style view DSL with decoupled chainable modifiers (`pathland-view`), declarative diff-based reactive emission (`pathland-engine`), host reader to a native-element description (`pathland-host`), opcode transport with network-batch encode/decode + time/size batching policy (`pathland-transport`), the WIT component world (`wit/pathland.wit`) + WASM guest component (`pathland-guest`) + host bindings/bridge (`pathland-wit-host`), golden conformance vectors (incl. raw-input EVENT and network-batch bytes), typed raw-input event encode/decode, `no_std` + wasm32 builds, zero-alloc steady-state emission. **Tests green across 6 crates.**
261: 
262: **Planned / deferred**: signals (Goal 2/#13), Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo (Goal 4/#15), GTK4 renderer refinements (Goal 5/#16), host → guest events over the network transport, TEXT_FIELD editing, image rendering.
263: 
264: ---
265: 
266: ## Quick Start
267: 
268: 1. Read this file and `spec/OPCODE.md`
269: 2. Run tests: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates)
270: 3. Build for wasm32: `RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
271: 4. Make small changes, verify they work
272: 
273: ---
274: 
275: ## Pathland Mindset
276: 
277: **Always remember**:
278: 1. Protocol is King
279: 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
280: 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
281: 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
282: 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
283: 
284: **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the reference implementation (`pathland-opcode`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

- Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
- **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
- **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes.

### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-gtk`)

The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
`id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:

- Rust demo links `pathland-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
  with an event closure.
- Java demo loads `pathland-gtk` as a `cdylib` via JNA and calls
  `pathland_gtk_run(host, on_event)`; button clicks round-trip as `EVENT`
  opcodes through the shared ring and are reported back via a JNA callback.

`pathland-gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
not be parsed as GTK options).

1: # Pathland Rust Workspace
2: 
3: The Rust core of Pathland: a **WASM guest engine** that emits the declarative
4: view structure as a fixed 16-byte opcode ring buffer into shared linear memory,
5: consumed by host renderers.
6: 
7: ```
8: crates/
9: ├── pathland-opcode/   # 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, bump arena, linear-memory layout (no_std)
10: ├── pathland-view/     # SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text/Button + decoupled
11: │                      #   chainable modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background) (no_std)
12: ├── pathland-engine/   # retained view tree -> declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes,
13: │                      #   diff-based reactive emission (zero-alloc steady state)
14: ├── pathland-host/     # host reader: ring -> native-element description (std layer)
15: ├── pathland-transport/# opcode transport: shared-memory ring + network batch encode/decode
16: │                      #   + batching policy + transport abstraction (RingTransport/FrameSource)
17: ├── pathland-guest/    # WASM guest component: retained tree + engine + emit/take-batch (browser)
18: ├── pathland-wit-host/ # WIT host bindings + DSL bridge (wasmtime embed, remote hosts)
19: ├── pathland-native/   # native C-ABI shim + NativeHost: flat world over a zero-copy shared ring
20: └── pathland-gtk-demo/ # GTK4 desktop demo: native engine -> zero-copy shared ring -> GtkBox/Label/Button
21: 
22: # Cross-language demo
23: ../java/pathland-demo/ # Java (Maven): SwiftUI-like DSL + JNA over pathland-native, zero-copy ring read
24: ```
25: 
26: ## Specification
27: 
28: - [`spec/OPCODE.md`](../../spec/OPCODE.md) — the 16-byte opcode protocol
29: - [`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`](../../spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors
30: - [`wit/pathland.wit`](../../wit/pathland.wit) — the WIT component world
31: 
32: ## Run tests
33: 
34: ```bash
35: PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo test
36: ```
37: 
38: ## Run the GTK desktop demo (native, zero-copy shared ring)
39: 
40: ```bash
41: PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo run -p pathland-gtk-demo
42: ```
43: 
44: Requires GTK4 (`brew install gtk4` on macOS).
45: 
46: ## Run the Java demo (cross-language, JNA over the native C-ABI shim)
47: 
48: ```bash
49: PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo build -p pathland-native
50: cd ../java/pathland-demo && mvn -q -Dpathland.rust.target=<lib/rust/target/debug> compile exec:java
51: ```
52: 
53: The Java app uses a SwiftUI-like DSL, drives the Rust engine via the flat
54: `pathland_native_*` C ABI (no per-component wrappers), and reads the resulting
55: opcodes **zero-copy** from the shared-memory ring. Verify headlessly with
56: `-Dexec.mainClass=demo.DemoHeadless`.
57: 
58: 
59: ## Build for wasm32
60: 
61: ```bash
62: RUSTC=~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustc \
63:   cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
64: ```
65: 
66: > The Homebrew `cargo` on PATH resolves a rustc without the wasm std. Use the
67: > rustup toolchain's rustc via `RUSTC=...` (or `rustup run stable cargo`).
68: 
69: ## Engine example
70: 
71: The engine emits declarative structure (no rects). A signal changes a property;
72: the next `emit` writes only the delta opcodes.
73: 
74: ```rust
75: use pathland_engine::Engine;
76: use pathland_opcode::{init_memory, Guest, MemoryLayout};
77: use pathland_view::{assign_ids, text, vstack, View, ViewExt};
78: 
79: let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
80: let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
81: init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
82: 
83: let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
84: let mut engine = Engine::new();
85: 
86: let mut root = vstack![text("Hello")]
87:     .spacing(4.0)
88:     .padding(8.0)
89:     .build();
90: assign_ids(&mut root, &mut 1);
91: 
92: guest.begin_frame();
93: engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // full structure
94: guest.end_frame();
95: 
96: root.properties.insert(pathland_opcode::property_id::SPACING, 12.0f32.to_bits());
97: 
98: guest.begin_frame();
99: engine.emit(&root, &mut guest).unwrap(); // exactly one SET_PROPERTY
100: guest.end_frame();
101: ```
102: 
103: Emission in the steady state allocates nothing; only changed nodes produce
104: opcodes, so an unchanged tree emits zero opcodes. Native renderers map the
105: structure onto their native elements (GTK4 widgets, DOM elements).
106: 
107: ## Network transport example
108: 
109: Frames emitted into the ring can be serialized into network batches and flushed
110: on a time/size policy (`BatchEncoder` / `Batcher`); a `BatchDecoder` rebuilds a
111: `Frame`-compatible view so the same `RenderTree::apply_frame` consumes batches
112: and shared-memory frames identically. See `spec/OPCODE.md#transport`.

Done. The Swing demo is gone and both demos now render through a shared GTK renderer, with events flowing through the opcode engine.

## What changed

**Events now go through the opcode engine** (your correction):
- `pathland-opcode`: added a **host→guest event ring** — a second 16-byte-slot ring in shared memory with `eventReadCursor`/`eventWriteCursor` (header `0x2A`–`0x3A`). `Host::send_event` encodes a raw input as an `EVENT` opcode; `Guest::drain_events` decodes it. Spec (`OPCODE.md`/`CONFORMANCE.md`) updated.
- `pathland-transport`/`pathland-native`: `send_input` now actually writes the event opcode (was stubbed); `drain_events` reads it back.

**Shared GTK renderer** (`pathland-gtk`, new rlib+cdylib):
- Incremental `GtkRenderer` (`id → gtk::Widget` retained map, delta-applied — no full rebuild) + `run`/`run_with_pump` owning the GTK app/window/main loop, pumping frames in and events out.
- C ABI `pathland_gtk_run(host, on_event)` for Java via JNA.

**Demos (no GTK/Swing usage)**:
- Rust `pathland-gtk-demo`: authors the DSL, emits into the ring, calls `pathland_gtk::run(...)` — zero `gtk::`/`glib::`/`pango::` imports.
- Java `demo/GtkDemo`: deleted `DemoApp` (Swing); drives the DSL via `pathland-native`, renders via `pathland_gtk_run`; button clicks round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes and come back through a JNA callback. Zero `javax.swing`/`java.awt`.

## Verified
- `cargo test`: all 20 suites green.
- `DemoHeadless`: `OK: ... 'Count: 8'`.
- Rust demo + Java `GtkDemo` both launch and stay running.

Two things to know:
1. **macOS main-thread requirement**: GTK must run on the main thread, and JBR runs Java `main()` on a non-main thread (`pthread_main_np()==0`). Run the Java demo with `MAVEN_OPTS="-XstartOnFirstThread"` (documented in `GtkDemo.java`, `README`, `AGENTS.md`).
2. `run_with_pump` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK so the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags aren't parsed as GTK options.
How do I run the rust demo

The Rust GTK demo doesn't need the `-XstartOnFirstThread` flag (Rust's main runs on the pthread main thread). Just:

```
cd lib/rust
PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo run -p pathland-gtk-demo
```

Both demos now run cleanly. The fix addressed **two** bugs:

1. **Infinite loop in the frame pump** — `RingTransport::next_frame()` recreates a fresh `Host` each call (resetting its `consumed` counter), so after draining the real frame it kept returning empty frames forever instead of `None`. `pump_once` looped forever inside `connect_activate`, never reaching `window.present()`. Fixed by adding a `start == end` guard in `Host::frames()` (pathland-opcode/src/lib.rs) so an already-drained ring returns no frame. Added a regression test `next_frame_returns_none_after_drain`.

2. **`RenderTree::root()` hardcoded node id 0** — the demos assign the root id 1, so `root_widget()` returned `None` and the window got no child. Fixed to find the node with `parent == None`.

Plus the earlier argv split: the Rust path now passes the real program args; the Java path passes a bare `["GtkDemo"]`.

feat: shared GTK4 renderer + bidirectional event ring

Introduce a single GTK4 renderer that both the Rust and Java demos use, and
route raw-input events through the opcode engine instead of side-channel
callbacks. Remove Swing entirely.

- pathland-opcode: add a host->guest event ring (second 16-byte-slot ring) with
  eventReadCursor/eventWriteCursor header fields; Host::send_event encodes a
  raw input as an EVENT opcode, Guest::drain_events decodes it. Fix
  Host::frames() so an already-drained ring returns no frame (was returning
  empty frames forever when a fresh Host reset its consumed counter).
- pathland-transport: RingTransport::send_input writes EVENT opcodes;
  RingTransport::drain_events reads them (was a stubbed BadInput).
- pathland-native: FrameSource/DriverTransport for NativeHost + drain_events.
- pathland-gtk (new rlib+cdylib): incremental GtkRenderer (id -> gtk::Widget
  delta sync) + run/run_with_pump owning the GTK app/window/main loop, pumping
  frames in and events out; C ABI pathland_gtk_run for Java via JNA. Passes an
  explicit argv to GTK so the embedding host's command line (JVM -cp/-D) is not
  parsed as GTK options.
- pathland-host: fix RenderTree::root() to find the parentless node (was
  hardcoded id 0).
- pathland-gtk-demo: author the DSL and render via pathland-gtk; no GTK APIs.
- Java demo: replace Swing DemoApp with GtkDemo (JNA over pathland_gtk_run);
  no Swing, no GTK APIs. Button clicks round-trip as EVENT opcodes.
- spec: document the event ring (OPCODE.md/CONFORMANCE.md); AGENTS.md/README
  updated.

Both demos render through the shared GTK renderer; cargo test green.
EOF
